questions.question: In India, ’National Science Day’ is celebrated on February 28 to mark the achievement of which scientist?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**C. V. Raman**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **National Science Day** is celebrated on **February 28** every year in India to commemorate the discovery of the **Raman Effect** by Sir **C. V. Raman** on this day in **1928**.
 
• Raman was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930** for his groundbreaking work on the scattering of light, which came to be known as the **Raman Effect**.
 
• The **Raman Effect** is a phenomenon in which light changes its wavelength when it passes through a transparent medium, leading to the discovery of molecular energy levels.
 
• The celebration of National Science Day is aimed at spreading awareness about the importance of **science, technology, and innovation** in daily life and encouraging the younger generation to pursue scientific careers.
 
• Every year, National Science Day is celebrated with a specific theme. For example, in **2023**, the theme was "**Global Science for Global Wellbeing**."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **C. V. Raman:**

 
 
• Born on **November 7, 1888**, in Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, India.
 
• He completed his education at **Presidency College, Madras**, and was a brilliant student in physics.
 
• In **1928**, he discovered the **Raman Effect**, which became a cornerstone of modern physics and spectroscopy.
 
• He was the first Indian to win a **Nobel Prize in Physics**, establishing India's global reputation in scientific research.
 
• He was also awarded the **Bharat Ratna**, India’s highest civilian honor, in **1954**.
 
 
 
• **Raman Effect:**
 
 
• The Raman Effect explains the scattering of light when it traverses a material medium and undergoes a change in energy and wavelength.
 
• This discovery opened up new avenues for studying molecular structures and has applications in fields such as **chemistry, material science, and biology**.
 
• The **Raman Spectroscopy** technique is widely used in various industries, including pharmaceuticals and environmental science.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Scientists Mentioned in the Options:**
 
 
• **Homi J. Bhabha:** Known as the **Father of India’s Nuclear Program**; he was instrumental in establishing the **Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)**.
 
• **Vikram Sarabhai:** Known as the **Father of the Indian Space Program**; he played a pivotal role in establishing **ISRO** (Indian Space Research Organisation).
 
• **A. P. J. Abdul Kalam:** Known as the **Missile Man of India** for his work on ballistic missile technology; he also served as the **11th President of India**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Science Day:**

 
 
• Started in **1986** upon the recommendation of the National Council for Science and Technology Communication (NCSTC).
 
• It is an occasion to honor the contributions of Indian scientists and promote the importance of **scientific research**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Raman Effect:**
 
 
• Used in **chemical analysis** to determine the composition of substances.
 
• Applied in **forensic science** for crime scene investigations.
 
• Widely utilized in **astronomy** to study the composition of distant celestial bodies.

questions.question: One Nation, One Subscription (ONOS) scheme, introduced on 1 January 2025 by which of the following ministry?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **One Nation, One Subscription (ONOS)** scheme was introduced by the **Ministry of Education** on **1 January 2025**.
 
• The initiative aims to provide **universal access** to academic resources such as **journals, research papers, and e-books** for students, researchers, and institutions across India.
 
• This scheme is expected to reduce the financial burden on educational institutions by centralizing the procurement of **educational and research resources**.
 
• It is designed to strengthen the **research ecosystem** in India, enabling both public and private institutions to access resources at a significantly lower cost.
 
• The initiative aligns with the goals of the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020**, which emphasizes equitable and inclusive access to education.

__
 
• **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020:**

 
 
• The NEP 2020 is a comprehensive framework aimed at transforming the Indian education system by **2030**.
 
• It focuses on **universal access**, **equity**, and **quality improvement** in education.
 
• The policy emphasizes the importance of **digital learning platforms** to ensure that knowledge is accessible to all.
 
 
 
• **Digital Library Initiative:**
 
 
• The ONOS scheme is a step towards the creation of a **National Digital Library** that will house resources from **Indian and global publishers**.
 
• It will cater to various fields, including **science, technology, arts, and humanities**.
 
 
 
• **Cost Efficiency:**
 
 
• Centralized subscription plans will significantly reduce the cost of accessing research materials for **educational institutions**.
 
• It will also eliminate the need for individual institutions to negotiate with publishers, ensuring **uniform access** across the country.
 
 
 
• **Implementation Agency:**
 
 
• The scheme will be implemented by the **Ministry of Education**, with support from government bodies such as the **University Grants Commission (UGC)** and **National Digital Library of India (NDLI)**.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• Similar initiatives, like the European Union’s **Open Access 2020**, aim to make research publications freely available to the public.
 
• The ONOS scheme will enable India to align with global standards in **open access and academic inclusivity**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ministry of Education:** The Ministry plays a key role in formulating policies and implementing schemes to improve India’s educational framework.
 
• The ONOS scheme is specifically targeted at addressing the **digital divide** in education by ensuring equitable access to academic resources.
 
• The scheme will also facilitate **collaborative research** and innovation by providing a common platform for researchers across the country.

questions.question: As per State of the Judiciary Report 2023, women constitute ______ of the working strength of the district judiciary.

questions.question: Which of the following species of big cat cannot roar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cheetah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cheetahs**, unlike other big cats such as tigers, leopards, and jaguars, **cannot roar**. Instead, they communicate with chirps, growls, purrs, and other vocalizations.
 
• The inability of cheetahs to roar is due to the anatomy of their voice box. They have a fixed structure in their larynx, which allows them to purr but not produce the deep, resonating roar typical of other big cats.
 
• The roaring ability in big cats is attributed to the presence of an elastic ligament in their hyoid bone, which cheetahs lack. This ligament is essential for producing the low-frequency sound of a roar.
 
• Leopards, tigers, and jaguars all belong to the genus **Panthera**, which is characterized by the ability to roar. Cheetahs, on the other hand, belong to the genus **Acinonyx**, which does not include roaring species.
 
• The cheetah's unique vocalizations, such as chirping, help them communicate with their cubs and other cheetahs in the wild, especially over short distances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Leopard:**

 
 
• Leopards belong to the genus **Panthera** and are capable of roaring.
 
• They are found in sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Asia, and the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Their roars are used for territorial marking and to warn off rivals or predators.
 
 
 
• **Tiger:**
 
 
• Tigers, also part of the genus **Panthera**, are known for their loud and powerful roars.
 
• They use their roar for communication, territorial marking, and mating calls.
 
• Tigers are mostly found in dense forests in Asia, including India, Siberia, and Southeast Asia.
 
 
 
• **Jaguar:**
 
 
• Jaguars are native to Central and South America and are part of the genus **Panthera**.
 
• They are capable of roaring, which helps them establish dominance and communicate with others.
 
• Jaguars are often found in tropical rainforests and other dense habitats.
 
 
 
• **Cheetah:**
 
 
• Cheetahs are classified under the genus **Acinonyx**, distinguishing them from roaring big cats.
 
• They are known for their extraordinary speed, capable of reaching up to **70 mph (112 km/h)** in short bursts.
 
• Cheetahs are typically found in savannas and grasslands of Africa and parts of Iran.
 
• Their social structure is different, with males often forming coalitions, while females are solitary or stay with their cubs.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The ability to roar in big cats is determined by the structure of their hyoid bone and the presence of an elastic ligament.
 
• Cheetahs, being the fastest land animals, rely more on speed and agility for hunting rather than roaring for territorial dominance or communication.
 
• The differences in vocal abilities among big cats highlight the diversity in their evolutionary adaptations, which are shaped by their respective habitats and lifestyles.
 
• Conservation efforts are crucial for all big cat species, as many face threats from habitat loss, poaching, and human-wildlife conflict.

questions.question: Who among the following was the first chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dr. Vikram A Sarabhai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dr. Vikram A Sarabhai** was the **founder and the first chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**, established in **1969**. He is regarded as the father of the Indian space program.
 
• He played a pivotal role in establishing the **Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR)** in **1962**, which later evolved into ISRO.
 
• Dr. Sarabhai's vision was to use **space technology for socio-economic development**. He emphasized the importance of using satellites for communication, education, and agricultural development in India.
 
• Under his leadership, India's first satellite, **Aryabhata**, was conceptualized, although it was launched later in **1975**.
 
• He collaborated with global space agencies, including **NASA**, to set up the **Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS)** in Kerala for launching sounding rockets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dr. Vikram A Sarabhai:**

 
 
• Born on **12 August 1919**, in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, he belonged to a prominent industrialist family.
 
• He was instrumental in setting up several scientific institutions in India, including the **Physical Research Laboratory (PRL)** in Ahmedabad in **1947**.
 
• He also contributed to the development of **India's nuclear power program** and worked closely with **Homi J Bhabha**.
 
• Dr. Sarabhai received several accolades, including the **Padma Bhushan (1966)** and **Padma Vibhushan (posthumously in 1972)**.
 
 
 
• **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO):**
 
 
• ISRO was established in **1969** under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). It became a part of the **Department of Space** in **1972**.
 
• ISRO's primary objective is to develop space technology and use its applications for various national tasks.
 
• It has launched numerous satellites like **INSAT**, **GSAT**, and **RISAT** for communication, weather forecasting, and remote sensing.
 
• ISRO's achievements include the **Mangalyaan mission (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013)** and the **Chandrayaan missions** to the Moon.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Prof. M G K Menon:** He was a renowned physicist who served as the Chairman of the Indian Space Commission but not the first chairman of ISRO.
 
• **Prof. Satish Dhawan:** He succeeded Dr. Sarabhai as the Chairman of ISRO in **1972** and contributed significantly to its growth, including the launch of the first Indian satellite, **Aryabhata**.
 
• **Homi J Bhabha:** Known as the **father of the Indian nuclear program**, he was instrumental in the establishment of atomic energy research in India but was not directly involved with ISRO.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **First Satellite:** India's first satellite, **Aryabhata**, was launched on **19 April 1975**, from the Soviet Union. It marked a significant milestone in India's space journey.
 
• **Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS):** Established in **1963**, TERLS was India's first rocket launching station, located in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala.

questions.question: What happens to the pressure when the area is reduced while keeping the force same?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pressure increases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pressure** is defined as the force exerted per unit area. It is mathematically expressed as:

 Pressure = Force/Area (P = F/A).
 
• If the **force remains constant**, and the area over which the force is applied is reduced, the pressure will **increase**. This is because pressure is inversely proportional to area.
 
• For example, when a sharp knife (smaller area) is used to cut an object, it applies more pressure compared to a blunt knife (larger area) for the same force applied.
 
• This principle is also utilized in **hydraulic systems**, where smaller areas are used to generate higher pressures.
 
• **Hence, when the area is reduced while keeping the force constant, the pressure increases.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of Pressure:**

 
 
• Pressure is a scalar quantity and is measured in units such as **Pascals (Pa)** in the SI system.
 
• 1 Pascal = 1 Newton per square meter (N/m²).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Pressure:**
 
 
• In **medical syringes**, the small cross-sectional area of the needle increases pressure, allowing the fluid to be easily injected or extracted.
 
• **Hydraulic brakes** in vehicles work on the principle of transmitting pressure through a fluid, using smaller areas to generate large forces.
 
• In **construction**, pile drivers use smaller areas to exert higher pressure for driving piles into the ground.
 
 
 
• **Real-Life Examples:**
 
 
• Walking on snow with flat shoes is difficult due to lesser pressure distribution, but snowshoes help distribute the pressure over a larger area, preventing sinking.
 
• High-heeled shoes exert greater pressure on the ground compared to flat-soled shoes because of their smaller contact area.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Context:**
 
 
• The formula P = F/A demonstrates the **inverse proportionality** between pressure and area when force is constant.
 
• This relationship is a fundamental concept in fluid mechanics and solid mechanics.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: Pressure decreases** - Incorrect. Since pressure is inversely proportional to area, reducing the area increases pressure, not decreases it.
 
• **Option 3: Pressure remains constant** - Incorrect. Pressure cannot remain constant if the area changes while the force is constant, as they are mathematically related.
 
• **Option 4: Pressure becomes zero** - Incorrect. Pressure can only become zero if the force is zero or the area approaches infinity, which is not the case here.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement about weight is correct?

I. Weight has only magnitude but no direction

II. Weight is a force acting vertically downwards
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement I:** "Weight has only magnitude but no direction" is incorrect. Weight is a **vector quantity** because it has both magnitude and direction. The direction of weight is always towards the center of the Earth (vertically downwards). Hence, *this statement is incorrect*.
 
• **Statement II:** "Weight is a force acting vertically downwards" is correct. Weight is defined as the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on an object. It acts in a vertical downward direction, towards the center of the Earth. Hence, *this statement is correct*.
 
• Weight is calculated using the formula **W = mg**, where:
 
 
• **W** is the weight of the object (measured in newtons).
 
• **m** is the mass of the object (measured in kilograms).
 
• **g** is the acceleration due to gravity (approximately **9.8 m/s²** on the surface of the Earth).
 
 
 
• Weight depends on both the **mass of the object** and the **gravitational field strength**. This means weight can vary depending on the location (e.g., on the Moon, weight is about 1/6th of that on Earth).
 
• Unlike weight, **mass** is a scalar quantity and remains constant irrespective of location. Mass only has magnitude but no direction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Difference between Mass and Weight:**

 
 
• **Mass:** It is the amount of matter in an object. Measured in **kilograms (kg)**. It is a scalar quantity and does not change with location.
 
• **Weight:** It is the force due to gravity acting on the mass of an object. Measured in **newtons (N)**. It is a vector quantity and depends on the gravitational field strength.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Force:** The force of attraction between two objects with mass. The weight of an object is a specific example of gravitational force.
 
• **Variation in Gravitational Field Strength:** The value of **g** (acceleration due to gravity) is not uniform across the Earth. It varies slightly with altitude, latitude, and the density of Earth's crust at different locations.
 
• **Weightlessness:** A condition experienced when there is no net force of gravity acting on an object. For example:
 
 
• Astronauts in orbit experience weightlessness because they are in free fall, moving along with the spacecraft under the influence of gravity.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Weight:**
 
 
• In designing elevators, aircraft, and bridges, engineers consider weight as a critical factor.
 
• Weight is crucial in understanding motion, stability, and balance in various physical systems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Weight on Different Celestial Bodies:** Weight varies depending on the gravitational pull of the celestial body. For example:

 
 
• On the Moon, the gravitational acceleration is about **1.62 m/s²**, which is approximately **1/6th** of Earth's gravity.
 
• On Jupiter, the gravitational acceleration is much stronger, approximately **24.79 m/s²**.
 
 
 
• **SI Unit of Weight:** The standard unit of weight is the **newton (N)**, named after Sir Isaac Newton, who formulated the law of gravitation.
 
• **Measurement of Weight:** Weight is commonly measured using a spring balance, which works based on the extension or compression of a spring under the influence of gravitational force.

questions.question: There are mainly ______ main processes of change of population.

__
 
• **Change in population** occurs primarily due to three main processes: **birth rate, death rate, and migration**. These are the fundamental factors influencing population dynamics.
 
• The **birth rate** refers to the number of live births per thousand people in a year. It contributes to the increase in population.
 
• The **death rate** is the number of deaths per thousand people in a year. A lower death rate leads to population growth, while a higher one can decrease it.
 
• **Migration** involves the movement of people from one place to another. It can be internal (within a country) or international (between countries). Migration affects the distribution and size of the population in different regions.
 
• These three processes—birth rate, death rate, and migration—are essential for understanding population trends and patterns globally. *Hence, the correct answer is 3.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Birth Rate:**

 
 
• The birth rate is expressed as the number of live births per 1,000 individuals per year.
 
• Countries with a high birth rate often experience rapid population growth, especially in developing nations.
 
• For example, in 2021, countries like **Niger** had one of the highest birth rates globally.
 
 
 
• **Death Rate:**
 
 
• It is the number of deaths per 1,000 individuals per year.
 
• Advancements in healthcare and sanitation have significantly lowered death rates worldwide, particularly in developed nations.
 
• For instance, countries like **Japan** have a low death rate due to their excellent healthcare system.
 
 
 
• **Migration:**
 
 
• Migration is categorized into immigration (moving into a new area) and emigration (moving out of an area).
 
• Migration can be driven by factors like economic opportunities, conflict, natural disasters, and education.
 
• For example, the **Syrian refugee crisis** saw millions of people migrating to other countries.
 
 
 
• **Population Growth:**
 
 
• Population growth is determined by the balance between birth rate and death rate, coupled with the net migration rate.
 
• Countries like **India** and **China** have seen significant population growth, while countries like **Japan** face population decline due to a low birth rate and high aging population.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Demographic Transition Theory:**

 
 
• This theory explains population change over time based on the birth and death rates.
 
• It has four stages: high stationary, early expanding, late expanding, and low stationary.
 
• Developed countries are in the last stage, while many developing nations are in the second or third stage.
 
 
 
• **Global Population Trends:**
 
 
• The world population reached **8 billion** in **2022**, as per the **United Nations**.
 
• Regions like **Sub-Saharan Africa** are expected to see the highest population growth by 2050.

questions.question: The sum of the gross value added of all the firms in an economy in a year is called _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gross Domestic Product**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country’s borders in a specific time frame, typically calculated annually.
 
• The **gross value added (GVA)** of all firms in an economy is a significant component of GDP calculation. GVA reflects the contribution of labor and capital in the production process.
 
• GDP can be calculated using three approaches: the **production approach** (based on GVA), the **income approach** (sum of incomes), and the **expenditure approach** (total spending).
 
• It serves as a primary indicator of a country’s economic performance and is widely used to compare the economic strength of nations globally.
 
• GDP includes data from various sectors like agriculture, manufacturing, services, and other industries, providing insights into the structural composition of the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**:

 
 
• GDP does not account for depreciation of capital assets, making it different from **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**, which includes depreciation adjustments.
 
• It is classified into **Nominal GDP** (measured at current market prices) and **Real GDP** (adjusted for inflation).
 
• India’s GDP is calculated by the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI)**, and the base year for calculation is currently **2011–2012**.
 
• In 2022, India ranked as the **fifth-largest economy globally** based on nominal GDP.
 
 
 
• **Gross Value Added (GVA)**:
 
 
• GVA measures the contribution of a sector to the economy, calculated as the difference between output and intermediate consumption.
 
• It provides detailed insights into sector-wise performance, making it useful for policymakers.
 
• GVA is a precursor to GDP, as GDP is derived by adding taxes and subtracting subsidies from GVA.
 
 
 
• **Net National Product (NNP)**:
 
 
• NNP is GDP minus depreciation, reflecting the net production of goods and services in an economy.
 
• It includes income earned by residents both domestically and abroad.
 
 
 
• **Gross Disposable Income (GDI)**:
 
 
• GDI refers to the total income available to the nation for spending or saving after accounting for taxes, subsidies, and transfers.
 
• It is a broader measure of economic well-being but does not directly represent production output.
 
 
 
• **Net National Income (NNI)**:
 
 
• NNI is calculated as NNP minus indirect taxes. It represents the actual income earned by the citizens.
 
• While important for understanding income distribution, NNI does not directly measure economic performance like GDP.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **GDP Calculation in India**:

 
 
• India’s GDP data is released quarterly by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**.
 
• The latest GDP figures are crucial for policy decisions by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and the Ministry of Finance.
 
 
 
• **World Economic Rankings**:
 
 
• As per the **World Bank** and **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**, GDP is used as a benchmark for international economic comparison.
 
• The **United States** remains the largest economy by nominal GDP, while **China** leads in GDP based on Purchasing Power Parity (PPP).
 
 
 
• **Applications of GDP Data**:
 
 
• GDP data is used for fiscal policy planning, monetary policy adjustments, and international trade negotiations.
 
• It helps identify growth trends and areas requiring government intervention.

questions.question: Which of the following hormone is associated with puberty in human males?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Testosterone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Testosterone** is the primary male sex hormone responsible for the development of secondary sexual characteristics in males during **puberty**.
 
• It is produced mainly by the **testes** in males, with a small amount being produced by the adrenal glands.
 
• Testosterone levels rise significantly during puberty, leading to changes such as the development of facial and body hair, deepening of the voice, and increased muscle mass.
 
• It also plays a vital role in sperm production and the maintenance of libido in males.
 
• Hormonal imbalances in testosterone levels can lead to various health issues, such as delayed puberty or fertility problems in males.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Adrenaline:**

 
 
• Adrenaline, also known as epinephrine, is a hormone released by the **adrenal glands** in response to stress or danger.
 
• It is part of the body's "fight or flight" response and helps in increasing heart rate, blood flow to muscles, and energy availability.
 
• Adrenaline is not linked to the changes that occur during puberty.
 
 
 
• **Oestrogen:**
 
 
• Oestrogen is the primary female sex hormone, produced mainly by the **ovaries**.
 
• It is responsible for the development of female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development and regulation of the menstrual cycle.
 
• Although males have small amounts of oestrogen, it does not play a significant role in male puberty.
 
 
 
• **Thyroxin:**
 
 
• Thyroxin is a hormone produced by the **thyroid gland** and is essential for regulating metabolism, growth, and development.
 
• It is not directly involved in the hormonal changes associated with puberty.
 
• An imbalance in thyroxin can lead to conditions such as hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, which may indirectly affect growth and development.
 
 
 
• **Testosterone:**
 
 
• It is a steroid hormone classified under **androgens**.
 
• Testosterone plays a critical role in the differentiation of male reproductive tissues such as the testes and prostate.
 
• It also influences behaviors such as aggression and competitiveness, which become more pronounced during puberty.
 
• Testosterone levels are typically higher in males than in females, contributing to the distinct physical differences between the sexes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of Testosterone in Puberty:**

 
 
• Testosterone is responsible for the **growth of the male reproductive organs**, including the penis and testes.
 
• It stimulates the production of **sperm** in the testes, a process called spermatogenesis.
 
• The hormone also contributes to the development of secondary sexual characteristics, such as a deeper voice and facial hair.
 
 
 
• **Age of Onset of Puberty:**
 
 
• In boys, puberty typically begins between the ages of **9 and 14 years**.
 
• The increase in testosterone levels during this period triggers various physical and emotional changes.
 
 
 
• **Testosterone and Health:**
 
 
• Low testosterone levels in males can lead to **delayed puberty**, reduced muscle mass, and fatigue.
 
• High testosterone levels may result in **aggressive behavior** or other health issues.

questions.question: Most of Ashoka’s edicts were composed in which language?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prakrit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Most of Ashoka’s edicts** were composed in the **Prakrit language**, which was the common language of the masses during that period.
 
• Prakrit was chosen because it was widely understood by ordinary people across the Mauryan Empire, making it easier to communicate the emperor’s messages.
 
• The edicts were inscribed on rocks and pillars, emphasizing **Dhamma (righteousness)**, moral values, and non-violence.
 
• While Prakrit was the primary language, some edicts were written in other scripts and languages, such as **Greek, Aramaic, and Sanskrit**, to address diverse communities.
 
• These inscriptions were written in the **Brahmi script**, the most prominent script of ancient India, and in some cases, the Kharosthi script was also used.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Prakrit Language:**

 
 
• Prakrit refers to a group of middle Indo-Aryan languages that were spoken in ancient and medieval India.
 
• It was the vernacular language as opposed to Sanskrit, which was considered the language of the elite and scholars.
 
• Examples of Prakrit dialects include **Magadhi, Shauraseni, and Ardhamagadhi**.
 
• It was widely used in Jain and Buddhist texts as well.
 
 
 
• **Ashoka’s Edicts:**
 
 
• The edicts of Emperor Ashoka are a collection of 33 inscriptions found across South Asia, including India, Nepal, Pakistan, and Afghanistan.
 
• They provide valuable historical information about Ashoka’s reign, his policies, and his adoption of Buddhism.
 
• The inscriptions focus on themes like **religious tolerance, welfare of people, animal rights, and ethical conduct**.
 
• They are considered one of the earliest examples of written communication by an Indian ruler.
 
 
 
• **Brahmi Script:**
 
 
• The Brahmi script is one of the oldest writing systems used in the Indian subcontinent and is the precursor to many modern scripts like Devanagari and Tamil.
 
• The script was used extensively in Ashoka’s inscriptions, especially in the **Prakrit language**.
 
• It is written from left to right and is phonetic in nature.
 
 
 
• **Other Languages in Ashoka's Inscriptions:**
 
 
• While Prakrit was the dominant language, some inscriptions in regions like Kandahar were written in **Greek and Aramaic**.
 
• This demonstrates Ashoka’s efforts to communicate with diverse linguistic and cultural groups within his empire.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• Ashoka’s inscriptions are a vital source of information about the **Mauryan Empire**, its administration, and the spread of Buddhism.
 
• They also reflect the emperor’s commitment to ethical governance and his conversion to Buddhism after the Kalinga War.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Languages of the Edicts:**

 
 
• Prakrit was the main language, written in Brahmi script.
 
• Greek and Aramaic were used in Afghanistan and other northwestern regions of the empire.
 
 
 
• **Kalinga War and Ashoka’s Transformation:**
 
 
• The Kalinga War (circa 261 BCE) was a turning point in Ashoka’s life and led to his adoption of Buddhism and the principles of non-violence.
 
• The edicts reflect his efforts to promote **Dhamma** (moral law) across his empire.
 
 
 
• **Key Locations:**
 
 
• Some significant sites of Ashoka’s inscriptions include **Sanchi, Sarnath, Dhauli, and Girnar**.
 
• The Kandahar inscription is notable for being written in Greek and Aramaic.
